name: Capgemini (Exceller: Analyst & Senior Analyst)
tagline: Pseudo-code, game-based aptitude, English and behavioural tests

overview.about: Capgemini hires engineering freshers through its Exceller programme. The standard Analyst offer comes from an online assessment of pseudo-code, game-based aptitude, English communication and behavioural profiling; an additional coding round can lead to a higher-package Senior Analyst offer. Each section is reported to be eliminatory. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.
eligibility: B.E./B.Tech/M.E./M.Tech/MCA (some drives include BCA/B.Sc) from eligible batches
Typically 60% or more in 10th, 12th/diploma and graduation (as reported)

pattern.note: Memory, reasoning, motion and grid challenges
Choose the statement that describes you better

overview.frequency: Campus drives and periodic off-campus Exceller drives

cards.title: What it tests
cards.body: About 30 MCQs where you trace short pseudo-code and pick the output. Loops, recursion, bitwise operators, arrays and basic OOP/DS questions. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Recursion sample
Loop sample
cards.body:
count = 0
for i = 1 to 20
  if i mod 4 == 0 and i mod 6 == 0: count = count + 1
print count → only 12 → 1

cards.title: Speed trick
cards.body: For loops with 100s of iterations, find the pattern after 3–4 iterations instead of tracing everything (e.g. count multiples, sum of AP).

cards.title: Common traps
points: Integer division truncation
Loop runs one fewer/more time than you think
Variable reassigned inside a nested loop
Pre- vs post-increment in conditions

cards.q:
a = 12, b = 10
a = a ^ b
print a
fun(n): if n == 0 return 0; return (n mod 2) + 10 * fun(n / 2). fun(6) = ?
sum = 0; for i = 1 to 100: if i mod 10 == 0: sum = sum + i. print sum

notes.p:
Capgemini's assessment includes a **pseudo-code round** (about 30 questions in roughly 30 minutes is commonly reported) that tests whether you can read code: loops, recursion, bitwise operators, arrays and functions in a C-like pseudo-language. It is often an elimination round, so accuracy matters. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

Method: build a **trace table**, watch integer division, and recognise patterns (swap via XOR, digit sum, bit counting) so you do not trace every step.

**Q1.** `a = 10, b = 4; a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b; print a, b` → XOR swap → **4 10**.

**Q2.** `f(n): if n == 0 return 0; return n mod 10 + f(n / 10)`; `f(4567)` = 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = **22**.

**Q3.** `x = 5; for i = 1 to 3: x = x + (x >> 1)` → 5 + 2 = 7 → 7 + 3 = 10 → 10 + 5 = **15**.

**Q4.** `count = 0; for i = 1 to 20: if (i & 1) == 0 and i mod 3 == 0: count++` → even multiples of 3 = multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18 → **3**.

**Q5.** `n = 13, c = 0; while n > 0: c = c + (n & 1); n = n >> 1` counts set bits; 13 = 1101 → **3**.

`a, b = 10, 4
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b
print(a, b)
f = lambda n: 0 if n == 0 else n % 10 + f(n // 10)
print(f(4567))
x = 5
for i in range(3):
    x = x + (x >> 1)
print(x)
print(sum(1 for i in range(1, 21) if (i & 1) == 0 and i % 3 == 0))
n, c = 13, 0
while n > 0:
    c += n & 1
    n >>= 1
print(c)`

Output:
`4 10
22
15
3
3`
Most pseudo-code answers depend on these rules:
points: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `~` NOT; `x & 1` tests odd/even.
`x << k` = x × 2ᵏ; `x >> k` = x ÷ 2ᵏ (floor, for non-negative x).
`n & (n − 1)` removes the lowest set bit; it is 0 only for powers of two (and 0).
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 = 3 in integer pseudo-code.
Precedence in C-like code: arithmetic before shifts before comparisons before `&`, `^`, `|`, then `&&`, `||`.
Loops from 1 to n are inclusive in most pseudo-code.
A variable passed 'by value' to a function does not change in the caller.
Recursion that prints before vs after the recursive call reverses the order.
Static/global variables persisting between calls.
Trace table for every non-trivial loop.
XOR swap, digit sum, set-bit count are common patterns.
Shifts multiply/divide by powers of two.
Watch inclusive loop bounds and integer division.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Game-based aptitude
cards.body: Short games replace classic quant MCQs: remember sequences, deduce rules from shapes, move objects on a grid, track motion. Each lasts a few minutes. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Common game types
points: Memory: recall growing sequences of tiles/digits
Inductive reasoning: find the rule linking shapes
Grid / switch challenges: plan moves under limits
Motion: route an object to a target in few moves

cards.title: Games strategy
cards.body: Read every instruction, use the practice round, stay calm after a wrong answer — difficulty usually adapts, and accuracy outweighs speed.

cards.title: Behavioural profiling
cards.body: Pairs of statements; choose which describes you better. Measures traits like teamwork, adaptability and drive. There are no 'right' answers, but consistency is checked.

cards.title: Behavioural strategy
cards.body: Answer honestly and quickly. Trying to guess the ideal profile often creates contradictions that hurt more than any single trait.

cards.title: English communication
cards.body: Grammar, sentence correction, vocabulary in context and reading comprehension, about 30 questions in 30 minutes.

cards.q: In a forced-choice behavioural test, the best approach is to:
options: Pick the 'most impressive' statement every time

cards.explain: Games measure reasoning and memory instead of classic aptitude questions.

notes.p:
Capgemini uses a **game-based aptitude test**: short, timed mini-games that measure memory, logic, speed and accuracy instead of traditional MCQs. Games reported in recent drives include **deductive logical thinking**, **grid challenge**, **motion challenge**, **inductive logical thinking**, **switch challenge** and **digit challenge**. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

Each game adapts or scores on both correctness and time, so a steady, accurate pace beats random fast clicking.
Each game rewards a different skill, so use a specific approach for each:
points: **Deductive logical thinking:** decide if a conclusion follows from given statements (like syllogisms). Draw quick Venn diagrams mentally; answer only from the statements.
**Grid challenge:** remember positions of dots on a grid while answering symmetry or rotation questions in between. Chunk positions into shapes (a line, an L) to remember them.
**Motion challenge:** slide blocks to move a ball into a hole in the fewest moves. Plan backwards from the hole before moving.
**Inductive logical thinking:** find which figure breaks the rule followed by the others (rotation, count, colour).
**Switch challenge:** find which switch code turned the input symbol order into the output order (see the example below).
**Digit challenge:** fill digits (without repeating) into blanks so an equation is true. Start with the operation that limits choices most (multiplication or the largest digit).

notes.p:
If the input is A B C D and the output is C A D B, the switch code lists, for each output position, which input position it came from: C was at 3, A at 1, D at 4, B at 2 → code **3142**. Practising this mapping makes the game fast:

`def switch_code(inp, out):
    return "".join(str(inp.index(s) + 1) for s in out)

def apply_code(inp, code):
    return [inp[int(c) - 1] for c in code]

print(switch_code(list("ABCD"), list("CADB")))
print(apply_code(list("ABCD"), "4213"))`

Output:
`3142
['D', 'B', 'A', 'C']`

This is a personality-style questionnaire (agree/disagree or pick the statement most like you). It checks traits such as teamwork, ownership, adaptability and integrity. There is no single right answer, but **inconsistent** answers (claiming opposite traits in similar questions) look bad.
points: Answer honestly and consistently; similar statements repeat with different wording.
Think as a professional at work, not as a student at home.
Avoid extreme answers on everything.
Do not over-think — the test is timed.
Clicking quickly without thinking — wrong answers can cost more than slow ones.
Losing grid positions while answering the in-between symmetry questions; rehearse the pattern silently.
Making unnecessary moves in the motion challenge; plan first.
Taking the test on a slow device or browser — use a stable laptop and internet connection.
Games score accuracy and speed together.
Grid: chunk dot positions; motion: plan backwards.
Switch: map each output symbol to its input position.
Digit: start from the most restrictive operation.
Behavioural: honest and consistent.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Senior Analyst coding
cards.body: Candidates who clear the main assessment may take an advanced coding test (about 2 problems). Clearing it can lead to a higher-package Senior Analyst offer.

cards.title: Sample coding task
cards.body:
Rotate an array right by k:
def rotate(a, k):
    k %= len(a)
    return a[-k:] + a[:-k]
rotate([1,2,3,4,5], 2) → [4,5,1,2,3]

cards.title: Technical interview
cards.body: Project, one language in depth, OOP, SQL, OS basics; sometimes cloud or testing basics. Be ready to write small programs on paper.

cards.title: HR interview
cards.body: Introduction, why Capgemini, relocation and shift readiness, a STAR story about teamwork or failure.

cards.title: Talk while you code
cards.body: Explain your approach before writing: brute force, then the better idea, then complexity. Silence makes interviewers guess.

cards.title: Common technical question
cards.body: "Difference between a primary key and a unique key?" Primary key: one per table, no NULLs. Unique key: many allowed, permits NULL (one in some DBMS).

cards.q: Which is true of a primary key?
cards.explain: Primary keys are unique and NOT NULL; only one per table.

notes.p: Capgemini hires freshers mainly as **Analyst** and, for stronger coders, **Senior Analyst** (higher package). Senior Analyst candidates face an additional **coding round** — commonly reported as 2 problems — before the interviews. After that come a **technical interview** and an **HR interview**. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

**Problem.** Rotate an N × N matrix 90° clockwise.

**Idea.** Transpose (swap a[i][j] with a[j][i]), then reverse each row. Both steps are in place, so space is O(1) extra and time is **O(N²)**.

`n = int(input())
m = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        m[i][j], m[j][i] = m[j][i], m[i][j]
for row in m:
    row.reverse()
for row in m:
    print(*row)`

Sample input:
`3
1 2 3
4 5 6
7 8 9`

Output:
`7 4 1
8 5 2
9 6 3`

**Q: What is a constructor? Can it be overloaded?** A: A special method that initialises an object; yes, with different parameter lists.

**Q: Difference between stack and heap memory?** A: Stack stores method frames and local variables (fast, automatic); heap stores objects (managed by GC or manually).

**Q: What is an index in a database?** A: A structure (often a B+ tree) that speeds up lookups at the cost of slower writes and extra space.

**Q: What is Agile?** A: An iterative way of building software in short sprints with frequent feedback; Scrum is a popular Agile framework.

**Q: Write SQL to find employees earning above the average.** A: `SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);`

**Q: Why Capgemini?** A: Cite specific points — its global consulting and technology presence, fresher training and your interest in its domains.

**Q: Describe a time you worked in a team.** A: STAR story with your own actions and a result.

**Q: Are you open to relocation and shifts?** A: Answer honestly; show flexibility where you can.

**Q: Walk me through your project's architecture.** A: Frontend → backend → database → deployment, one line each, then your module in detail.

**Q: Puzzle — you have 8 identical-looking balls, one heavier, and a balance. Minimum weighings?** A: 2 (weigh 3 vs 3; if equal, weigh the remaining 2; if not, weigh 1 vs 1 from the heavier three).

**Q: Your teammate is not doing their part close to a deadline. What do you do?** A: Talk privately first, understand the issue, offer help, and inform the lead early if the deadline is at risk.

**Q: What would you do in your first 90 days?** A: Learn the project and tools, deliver small tasks reliably, ask for feedback, and complete required trainings.

points: Claiming skills in your resume you cannot code live.
Blaming teammates in project or conflict stories.
Saying you plan to leave for higher studies soon after joining.
Senior Analyst: extra coding round.
Matrix rotation: transpose + reverse rows.
Revise OOP, memory, indexing, Agile, SQL subqueries.
Prepare STAR stories for HR.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.
